text: When I first walked into the robotics lab at Jefferson High in the fall of 2022, I honestly did not really know what a servo motor was, and I think I was the only freshman who had never written a single line of code. Our team captain, Priya Raman, handed me a laptop and told me that I would be in charge of the autonomous routine for the regional qualifier in March. At first I was very nervous and I kind of panicked, because I felt like everyone else on the team already knew so much more than I did. Over the next four months, I basically spent almost every single lunch period in the lab, reading documentation and testing the same twelve lines of code over and over again. When our robot finally scored all six points on its own during the qualifier, I realized that I actually liked the slow, frustrating process of figuring things out for myself. That is the kind of learning I want to keep doing at Carleton.

My grandmother's kitchen in Fresno was the first place where I learned that cooking is really a kind of conversation. Every Sunday, she would make tamales for the whole family, which usually meant around twenty people, and every Sunday she would insist that I help her spread the masa on the corn husks. At first, I thought it was very boring and repetitive, and honestly I would have much rather been playing video games with my cousins in the living room. But she always told me stories while we worked, about growing up in Michoacán, about the bakery her father owned, and about the long bus ride she took to California in 1974 with only two suitcases. I started to realize that the stories were the real reason she wanted me there. In a way, the tamales were just an excuse for us to spend time together and talk about things that she would not otherwise bring up. When she got sick last winter and could no longer stand at the counter for very long, I took over the spreading and the folding, and she sat at the table and told me which husks were too small. I think that was the moment when I understood that I was not only learning a recipe but also learning how to listen to someone carefully. Now, whenever I cook for my friends, I find myself asking them questions and waiting for the answers, the same way she always did with me. It is something that I want to bring with me to college, because I believe that the best conversations often happen when people are working side by side on something simple.

For the past three summers, I have worked at the Riverside Public Library as a volunteer reading tutor for kids between the ages of six and ten. When I first started, I honestly thought that the job would mostly consist of reading picture books out loud and helping kids sound out simple words. It turned out to be much more complicated than that. Many of the kids who came to the program were really behind in reading, and some of them had already decided, at the age of seven, that they were just bad at it and that there was no point in trying. One boy, Marcus, refused to read anything at all for the first two weeks. He would sit at the table with his arms crossed and stare at the wall whenever I opened a book. I tried a lot of different things in order to get him interested, like comic books, joke books, and even the instruction manual for a video game he liked, but nothing seemed to work at all. Then one afternoon I noticed that he was drawing a very detailed picture of a shark on the back of a worksheet. I asked him if he wanted to make his own book about sharks, and he said yes, which was the first time he had really agreed to anything. Over the next six weeks, we wrote a twelve-page book together, one sentence at a time, and he read every single sentence out loud to me, sometimes three or four times, until he was satisfied with it. On the last day of the program, he read the whole book to his mother in front of the other kids, and she cried. I learned from Marcus that people are usually not unwilling to learn; they are just waiting for a reason that matters to them. That lesson has changed the way that I approach tutoring, and it has also changed the way I think about my own learning, because I now try to find the shark in every subject that I find difficult.

I lost my first debate tournament so badly that the judge wrote only one sentence on my ballot: "Slow down and say what you mean." I was a sophomore at the time, and I had spent nearly three weeks preparing a case on whether cities should ban cars from their downtown areas. I had collected something like forty pages of evidence, including studies from Copenhagen and Bogotá, and I was completely convinced that the sheer amount of research I had done would be more than enough to win. Instead, I spoke so fast that I ran out of breath halfway through my first speech, and when my opponent asked me a simple question about bus routes, I froze and started reading a random quote that had nothing at all to do with what she had asked me. I remember sitting on the bus ride home and feeling honestly embarrassed, not because I had lost, but because I knew that I had not really understood my own argument. I had memorized facts without actually thinking about how they connected to each other.

Over the next year, my coach, Mr. Delgado, made me practice something he called the one-minute version. Before every round, I had to explain my entire case to him in sixty seconds, without notes, in plain language that my little brother could understand. At first, I found this incredibly frustrating, because it felt like I was throwing away most of the research that I had worked so hard to find. But slowly I started to notice that the one-minute version forced me to decide what actually mattered and what was just there to make me feel prepared. By the end of my junior year, I had won four tournaments and placed second at the state championship in Sacramento. More importantly, though, I had learned to stop hiding behind information. I now use the one-minute version for almost everything I do, from writing history essays to explaining a math problem to a friend who is stuck. It has taught me that being clear is not the same thing as being simple, and that real understanding usually means being able to leave things out. I think that this habit of asking myself what I actually mean will be one of the most useful things that I bring to college, especially in classes where the readings are long and the ideas are complicated and it would be easy to get lost in all of the details.

The summer before my junior year, I got a job at Hendricks Hardware, a small family-owned store on Main Street that has been open since 1958. I applied mostly because it was close to my house and because I needed money for a used car, and I honestly did not expect to learn very much there. On my first day, the owner, Mrs. Hendricks, who is seventy-three years old and still works six days a week, handed me a red apron and told me that my job was not to sell things but to solve problems. At the time, I thought that was just something that store owners say. I quickly found out that she really meant it.

Customers would come in with a broken piece of something wrapped in a paper towel and ask me if we had a replacement, and most of the time I had absolutely no idea what the piece even was. In the beginning, I would just walk them over to Mrs. Hendricks or to Dale, the assistant manager, who seemed to know the name and location of every single one of the roughly eleven thousand items in the store. But after a few weeks, I started paying closer attention to the questions they asked the customers. They never started by looking for the part. Instead, they always asked what the customer was trying to do, what had happened, and what they had already tried. I realized that the questions were actually more important than the answer, because half the time the customer did not need the part they had brought in at all.

One afternoon, a man came in looking for a new faucet because his kitchen sink was leaking, and he was clearly frustrated and in a hurry. Instead of selling him a faucet for eighty-nine dollars, I asked him a few questions, and it turned out that the leak was coming from a worn-out washer that cost about forty cents. I showed him how to replace it, and he came back the next week just to tell me that it had worked. That small moment made me feel more useful than almost anything I had done in school up to that point.

Working at Hendricks taught me that expertise is often less about knowing everything and more about knowing what to ask. It also taught me to be patient with people who are stressed, because most of them are not actually angry at you; they are just tired of a problem that they cannot solve on their own. I have carried this into other parts of my life as well, like when I help my younger sister with her homework or when I work on group projects at school. I now try to start with questions instead of answers. I still have the red apron, and I still think about what Mrs. Hendricks said on my first day, because I believe that solving problems for people is one of the most meaningful kinds of work there is.

I was eleven years old when my father brought home a box of broken telescope parts that he had bought for fifteen dollars at a yard sale in Modesto. He set the box down on our kitchen table, looked at me, and said, "I think we can fix this." Neither of us had ever built anything more complicated than a bookshelf, and I am fairly sure that neither of us really knew what a focal length was. But over the next two years, that box became the center of almost every weekend we spent together.

At first, our progress was very slow and honestly kind of discouraging. The main mirror had a long scratch across it, the tube was dented in two places, and several of the screws that held the eyepiece in place were missing entirely. We watched dozens of videos online, borrowed library books with titles like Amateur Telescope Making, and made at least three separate trips to the hardware store every month in order to find the right parts. Honestly, there were times when it felt like we spent more time looking for parts than actually building anything. My father worked long shifts as a nurse at the county hospital, so most of our work happened late on Saturday nights, after he had slept for a few hours and I had finished my homework. I remember the smell of the polishing compound and the sound of the radio playing old Mexican ballads while we took turns grinding the mirror by hand, one slow circle after another, for what felt like hundreds of hours.

There were many nights when I wanted to give up. Once, after we had spent almost an entire month regrinding the mirror, I accidentally dropped it on the garage floor, and a small chip broke off the edge. I was sure that my father would be angry, or at least disappointed, and I started apologizing before he even looked up. Instead, he picked up the mirror, turned it over in his hands, and told me that the chip was on the outside edge, where the light barely mattered. Then he said something that I still think about almost every day: "Most mistakes are on the edge. Keep going."

We finished the telescope in the spring of 2021, during my eighth-grade year. The first object we pointed it at was Saturn, and I will never forget how small and sharp the rings looked, like someone had drawn them on the glass with a very fine pen. My father and I stood in our backyard in the cold for over an hour, taking turns at the eyepiece and saying almost nothing, because there was really nothing that needed to be said.

Since then, that telescope has gone with me almost everywhere. I started an astronomy club at my high school, which now has twenty-six members, and we hold free viewing nights in the parking lot of the public library twice a month. Some nights only three people show up, and other nights the line stretches all the way to the sidewalk. I have shown Saturn to little kids, to tired parents, and to an old man who told me he had wanted to see it since he was a boy in Guatemala. Every time someone gasps when they first look through the eyepiece, I think about the yard sale box and about all of the nights when my father and I almost gave up.

Building that telescope taught me that patience is not the same as waiting. It is the decision to keep working on something even when the progress is too slow to see. It also taught me that I do not have to know how to do something before I start; I only have to be willing to learn it one step at a time. When I arrive at college, I want to study physics and engineering, and I know that there will be problems that seem as hopeless as a scratched mirror in a dented tube. When that happens, I plan to remember my father's words about mistakes on the edge, and I plan to keep going.
